title: Default Off Should Be the Norm in Every School
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that a default off stance toward classroom devices should become a national norm, so that students expect a teacher, classmates, and something worth thinking about before any screen opens. Building on his earlier piece on default off in practice, he turns the idea into a shared commitment across school leaders, teachers, students, and families. For leaders, he calls for clear expectations, attention to accessibility, time for teams to audit how much of the school day assumes being online, walkthroughs that ask students to explain what the tool is doing for them, and scrutiny of ed-tech products themselves. For teachers, he recommends starting with one upcoming lesson, assigning each tool a job, and making device transitions explicit and purposeful. He insists that accessibility tools remain in place as legitimate purposes, and that families be told plainly what the school promises. The piece concludes with six CC-licensed posters and a call for adults everywhere to be able to explain how chosen tools serve a child's learning.
points: Marcinek's rule of thumb is that devices stay closed or put aside until there is a specific instructional reason to use them.
He warns that if every opening question, text, and submission requires a screen, a school has made being online a condition of participation.
Leaders are urged to examine ed-tech products for the distractions they introduce and to create a process for reconsidering tools that get in the way.
Accessibility tools such as text-to-speech are explicitly protected as purposeful device use within a default off culture.
quotes: A student should walk into a classroom expecting to encounter a teacher, classmates, and something worth thinking about. The device can be available. Whether it opens should depend on what the learning requires.
For school leaders, start by making the expectation clear: classroom devices stay closed or put aside until there is a specific reason to use them.
If students need a screen to see the opening question, read every assignment, access every text, and submit every piece of work, you have made being online a condition of participation.

Look at the distractions it introduces, the quality of its feedback, and the demands it places on students' attention. Give teachers a way to raise concerns and a process for reconsidering tools that are getting in the way.
A device may earn a place for part of the lesson, for an extended project, or for a particular student's needs. Some lessons will work well with the devices put aside throughout.
A student using text-to-speech, communication software, or another accessibility tool may need a device while classmates are working on paper or talking. That use has a purpose.
Wherever a child goes to school, the adults should be able to explain how the tools they choose serve that child's learning.
